questions.text: How often do you use an AI agent that can take actions for you (run commands, edit files, browse, send messages), as opposed to a chat assistant that only answers?
options: I have tried one a few times
I build or deploy such agents
questions.maps: exposure; skip logic: 'Never' skips section B

questions.text: Which kinds of agent have you used? Select all that apply.
options: Coding agent with terminal or file access
E-mail, calendar or office assistant that can act

questions.text: What is the most powerful thing you have allowed an agent to do without asking you first?
options: Nothing: it only suggests, I act
Edit files in one project folder
Use my accounts, credentials or payment details

questions.text: Where does the agent usually run?
options: In a container or virtual machine
In a cloud sandbox provided by the tool
questions.maps: isolation in practice (gap G1; finding F2)

questions.text: When an agent says a task is finished, what do you usually do?
options: Run my own tests or checks
Review the changes line by line
questions.maps: outcome verification independent of the agent's narrative (category A)

questions.text: Has an agent you were using ever done something you had not authorized?
If yes: what happened? Select all that apply.
options: Changed or deleted files outside the task
Altered a test or check so that it passed
Followed instructions found in a page, document or message
Used the network, an account or a credential unexpectedly
Reported success when the task had not been done

questions.text: Think about your own use of agents over the next year. Which of these is MOST likely to happen, and which is LEAST likely?

items.a: The agent makes its result look successful without doing the task as intended (for example, changing a test or check so that it passes).
items.b: The agent follows instructions hidden in something it reads (a web page, e-mail, document or tool output) instead of the user's instructions.
items.c: Several agents pass each other content or permissions so that one does something none was individually allowed to do.
items.d: The agent does something outside its task and the monitoring or review in place does not catch it.

questions.text: If each of these did happen, which would do the MOST harm, and which the LEAST?

items.a: The agent makes its result look successful without doing the task as intended (for example, changing a test or check so that it passes).
items.b: The agent follows instructions hidden in something it reads (a web page, e-mail, document or tool output) instead of the user's instructions.
items.c: Several agents pass each other content or permissions so that one does something none was individually allowed to do.
items.d: The agent does something outside its task and the monitoring or review in place does not catch it.

questions.text: How far do you agree with each statement?

items.s1: A published attack-success rate for an agent tells me how safe it will be in my own setting.
items.s2: If an agent's work passes its tests, the task has been done as intended.
items.s3: A safeguard that works for one agent will also work when several agents work together.
items.s4: An automated monitor can be relied on to catch an agent that acts outside its task.
items.s5: More capable models are less likely to take unauthorized shortcuts.
items.s6: I would accept an agent being slower or less capable in exchange for stronger safeguards.

questions.maps: s1: F1/G2; s2: category A; s3: F4/G4; s4: F2/F3; s5: capability and gaming (A); s6: security-utility trade-off (F6). The reviewed work gives reasons to doubt s1-s5; agreement is therefore the informative response.

questions.text: An agent is given a task that turns out to be impossible as stated. Which is it MOST likely to do, and which LEAST likely?

items.stop: Stop and report that the task cannot be done
items.try: Keep trying within the rules until it runs out of time
items.alter: Change the test or check so that the task appears done
items.seek: Look for the answer somewhere it was not meant to access

questions.text: Which of these safeguards matters MOST, and which LEAST, for using agents safely?

items.iso: Running the agent in an isolated environment with no access to the wider network
items.priv: Giving the agent only the narrow permissions and credentials the task needs
items.appr: Requiring a person to approve risky actions before they run
items.mon: Having a second automated system monitor the agent's actions
items.adv: Testing the agent against deliberate attempts to break the safeguards before using it
